unit.title: Angles
unit.blurb: Comparing angles, right angles, acute and obtuse angles, and estimating the size of angles in degrees.
unit.subject: maths

O1.t: Compare angles with a right angle and order angles by size.

O2.t: Classify angles as acute, right or obtuse.

O3.t: Estimate the size of angles in degrees.

p: An **angle** is an amount of turn. A **right angle** is a quarter turn, **90°**. A straight line is two right angles, **180°**.
To compare angles, look at how far one arm turns from the other – not at how long the arms are.

lesson.t: Why angle size is about turn
p: An angle measures how far one arm turns from the other. Long arms do not make an angle bigger; only the turn does.

lesson.q: Angle A has short arms but a big turn. Angle B has long arms but a small turn. Which is bigger?
steps: Ignore the length of the arms

p: Look only at the turn between the arms.
Compare each angle with a right angle.
Order them from smallest to largest turn.
Longer arms do not make a bigger angle.

p: An **acute** angle is less than 90°. A **right** angle is exactly 90°. An **obtuse** angle is more than 90° but less than 180°.

lesson.t: Why we compare with a right angle
p: A right angle is 90°. Acute angles are smaller than a right angle and obtuse angles are between a right angle and a straight line (180°).

lesson.q: Is a 120° angle acute or obtuse?

p: Compare it with a right angle (90°).
Smaller → acute; equal → right angle.
Bigger but less than 180° → obtuse.
Remember: 'a cute little angle' is small – less than 90°.

p: Use angles you know to estimate: **90°** (right angle), **45°** (half a right angle), **180°** (straight line).
An angle a bit less than a right angle might be about 80°; halfway between 90° and 180° is about 135°.
Knowing 90° (a quarter turn) and 45° (half of that) gives us landmarks. We judge where a new angle sits between them.

lesson.q: An angle is a bit more than half a right angle. Estimate its size.

p: Compare it with 90°.
Compare it with 45° (half a right angle).
Give a sensible estimate in degrees.
If an angle is obtuse, your estimate must be more than 90°.
